Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN) -- Federal, state and municipal agencies staged an elaborate drill in the waters off New York City on Tuesday to prepare for the possibility of a nuclear or dirty-bomb attack from the water. A U.S. Coast Guard vessel passes a container ship in New York Harbor as part of Tuesday's terror drill. "We're a big city, and there are vulnerabilities," said Ray Kelly, commissioner of the New York Police Department. Agencies involved in Tuesday's test  emphasized they did not undertake it because of a specific threat against the city. However, Kelly said the city was taking no chances after a proclamation years ago by Osama bin Laden. "We do know that Osama bin Laden several years ago obtained a fatwah to use nuclear weapons, and our goal is to make certain that that fatwah does not come to fruition," he said. In addition to increasing various agencies' preparedness for a seaborne radiological attack, Kelly said Tuesday's well-publicized drill was meant to deter those who would perpetrate such an attack. "It pays to advertise to a certain extent. We want anyone who would do us harm to know that we're out there, that we have the capability to detect," Kelly said. Eight government agencies participated in the drill, ranging from the NYPD to the U.S. Coast Guard. The exercise took place at the entrance of New York Harbor, just south of the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge linking Staten Island to Brooklyn. Per the drill's plan, eight boats were to cross a checkpoint set up by authorities. They were on the lookout for abnormally high concentrations of radioactivity -- a telltale sign of an improvised nuclear device or a radiological dispersal device, more familiarly known as a dirty bomb. Some of the boats were decoys with no radioactive substances aboard, while others had actual radioactive isotopes planted in them. A radioactivity detector in the hull of the authorities' boats was to identify which vessels had radioactive substances in them. The devices are highly sensitive -- so much so that people who have recently had certain medical treatments can set them off. It was up to the authorities participating in the drill to sort the good boats from the bad -- and to intercept the bad. Only minutes into the six-hour exercise, equipment aboard a police boat detected radioactivity within a small white pleasure craft passing through the checkpoint. Two patrol vessels then converged on the pleasure craft, while officials began to question the driver and his two passengers. Soon after, authorities boarded the boat and used a radiation detector, officially known as a radiological isotope identification detector, to produce a "spectrum" of the radiological material. They then transmitted the spectrum to the Department of Homeland Security's Joint Analysis Center (JAC) in Washington to determine precisely what radiological material was aboard the boat. Within moments, the JAC radioed back with a positive identification: Caesium-137, an industrial radioactive isotope that if used in large enough quantities could power a devastating dirty bomb. Sure enough, when a separate boat containing press and police officers sidled up to the apprehended craft soon afterward, the portable radioactivity detectors of officers onboard began to sound excitedly. NYPD Sgt. Art Mogil said that, in part, the agencies chose to practice on leisure craft to illustrate that radiological weapons could be transported in deceptively benign-looking boats. "It doesn't require a large vessel. A device can be just a few pounds and still be a major threat," Mogil said. James Waters, counterterrorism chief for the NYPD, said exercises like Tuesday's were vital because the stakes involved are so high. "Someone bringing in a radiological or nuclear device would be very serious if not catastrophic," he said. On an average day, not all incoming maritime traffic in New York City is subjected to the radioactivity tests performed at Tuesday's drill. An NYPD official declined to specify what percentage of boats normally undergo such screening.

A U.S. Coast Guard vessel passed a container ship in New York Harbor as part of Tuesday’s terror drill.

“We’re a big city, and there are vulnerabilities,” said Ray Kelly, commissioner of the New York Police Department.

Agencies involved in Tuesday’s exercise emphasized that it was not undertaken in response to any specific threat against the city. However, Kelly said New York was taking no chances in light of a proclamation issued years ago by Osama bin Laden.

“We do know that Osama bin Laden several years ago obtained a fatwah to use nuclear weapons, and our goal is to make certain that that fatwah does not come to fruition,” he said.

In addition to strengthening the preparedness of various agencies for a seaborne radiological attack, Kelly said Tuesday’s well-publicized drill was intended to deter anyone who might attempt such an attack.

“It pays to advertise to a certain extent. We want anyone who would do us harm to know that we’re out there, that we have the capability to detect,” Kelly said.

Eight government agencies participated in the drill, ranging from the NYPD to the U.S. Coast Guard. The exercise took place at the entrance to New York Harbor, just south of the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, which links Staten Island and Brooklyn.

Under the drill’s plan, eight boats were to pass through a checkpoint established by authorities. Officials were watching for abnormally high concentrations of radioactivity — a telltale sign of an improvised nuclear device or a radiological dispersal device, more commonly known as a dirty bomb.

Some of the boats served as decoys and carried no radioactive substances, while others had actual radioactive isotopes placed aboard. A radioactivity detector mounted in the hull of the authorities’ boats was designed to identify which vessels contained radioactive materials.

The devices are highly sensitive — so sensitive that people who have recently undergone certain medical treatments can trigger them. It was up to the authorities participating in the drill to distinguish the harmless boats from the dangerous ones — and to intercept the latter.

Only minutes into the six-hour exercise, equipment aboard a police boat detected radioactivity in a small white pleasure craft passing through the checkpoint. Two patrol vessels then converged on the craft as officials began questioning the driver and his two passengers.

Soon afterward, authorities boarded the boat and used a radiation detector, officially known as a radiological isotope identification detector, to generate a “spectrum” of the radiological material. They then transmitted the spectrum to the Department of Homeland Security’s Joint Analysis Center (JAC) in Washington to determine precisely what radiological material was aboard.

Within moments, the JAC radioed back with a positive identification: Caesium-137, an industrial radioactive isotope that, in sufficiently large quantities, could power a devastating dirty bomb.

Indeed, when a separate boat carrying members of the press and police officers pulled alongside the apprehended craft shortly afterward, the portable radioactivity detectors carried by officers onboard began sounding excitedly.

NYPD Sgt. Art Mogil said the agencies chose, in part, to conduct the exercise using leisure craft to demonstrate that radiological weapons could be transported in deceptively benign-looking boats.

“It doesn’t require a large vessel. A device can be just a few pounds and still be a major threat,” Mogil said.

James Waters, the NYPD’s counterterrorism chief, said exercises like Tuesday’s are vital because the stakes are so high.

“Someone bringing in a radiological or nuclear device would be very serious if not catastrophic,” he said.

NEW YORK (CNN) — On Tuesday, federal, state and local authorities carried out a large-scale exercise in the waters near New York City, simulating preparations for a possible nuclear or “dirty bomb” strike launched from the water.

As part of the terrorism-response drill, a U.S. Coast Guard boat moved past a container ship in New York Harbor.

“We’re a big city, and there are vulnerabilities,” said Ray Kelly, the New York Police Department commissioner.

Officials from the agencies taking part stressed that the operation was not prompted by any particular threat to New York City. Still, Kelly said the city was unwilling to be complacent, citing a declaration made years earlier by Osama bin Laden.

“We do know that Osama bin Laden several years ago obtained a fatwah to use nuclear weapons, and our goal is to make certain that that fatwah does not come to fruition,” Kelly said.

Kelly explained that the highly visible drill was intended not only to improve the readiness of multiple agencies for a radiological attack arriving by sea, but also to discourage anyone considering such an assault.

“It pays to advertise to a certain extent. We want anyone who would do us harm to know that we’re out there, that we have the capability to detect,” he said.

Eight government organizations joined the exercise, including the NYPD and the U.S. Coast Guard. The operation was conducted at the entrance to New York Harbor, just south of the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, which connects Staten Island and Brooklyn.

Under the scenario, eight boats were scheduled to pass through a checkpoint established by authorities. Officials were searching for unusually elevated radiation levels, which could indicate the presence of either an improvised nuclear device or a radiological dispersal device, commonly called a dirty bomb.

Some vessels in the drill served as decoys and carried no radioactive material. Others had real radioactive isotopes placed aboard them. Radiation-detection equipment mounted in the hulls of official boats was supposed to determine which vessels contained radioactive substances.

The detectors are extremely sensitive — sensitive enough that people who recently received certain medical treatments can trigger them. The task for authorities in the exercise was to distinguish harmless boats from threatening ones, then stop the dangerous vessels.

Just minutes after the six-hour drill began, instruments on a police boat picked up radiation from a small white recreational boat traveling through the checkpoint. Two patrol boats moved in on the craft, and officials began questioning the operator and his two passengers.

Shortly afterward, officers boarded the boat and used a radiation detector — formally called a radiological isotope identification detector — to generate a “spectrum” of the radioactive material. That spectrum was sent to the Department of Homeland Security’s Joint Analysis Center, or JAC, in Washington, so analysts could determine exactly what substance was on board.

The JAC responded within moments with a positive identification: Caesium-137, an industrial radioactive isotope that, in sufficient quantity, could be used to create a highly destructive dirty bomb.

When another boat carrying reporters and police officers later pulled alongside the intercepted craft, portable radiation detectors carried by officers on board began sounding rapidly.

NYPD Sgt. Art Mogil said one reason officials chose to train with pleasure boats was to demonstrate that radiological weapons could be hidden and moved in vessels that appear harmless.

“It doesn’t require a large vessel. A device can be just a few pounds and still be a major threat,” Mogil said.

James Waters, the NYPD’s counterterrorism chief, said drills like Tuesday’s are essential because the possible consequences are so severe.

“Someone bringing in a radiological or nuclear device would be very serious if not catastrophic,” he said.

On a typical day, New York City does not subject every incoming boat to the type of radiation screening used during Tuesday’s exercise. An NYPD official would not say what share of maritime traffic is normally checked in that way.

**Coast Guard, NYPD Test Radiation Detectors on New York Harbor Boats to Guard Against Dirty-Bomb Threat**

*By Staff Writer*  
*New York City*

The U.S. Coast Guard, the New York Police Department and a coalition of federal, state and local agencies conducted a maritime security exercise in New York Harbor this week, testing radiation-detection equipment aboard patrol boats as part of ongoing efforts to prevent a potential seaborne dirty-bomb attack.

The drills, held in waterways around Lower Manhattan, Staten Island and the Brooklyn waterfront, involved multiple vessels equipped with sensors designed to detect radioactive material that could be hidden on a boat, barge or cargo vessel. Officials said the exercise was not in response to a specific threat, but rather part of routine preparedness in one of the nation’s busiest and most visible ports.

“New York Harbor is a critical transportation and commercial hub, and we train regularly to make sure we can identify and respond to potential hazards before they reach the city,” a Coast Guard official said. “These exercises help ensure that our teams and our partner agencies can operate together quickly and effectively.”

The NYPD’s Harbor Unit, Counterterrorism Bureau and Emergency Service Unit participated alongside the Coast Guard, the Department of Homeland Security, Port Authority police, the Fire Department and other regional partners. Crews practiced screening vessels, sharing detection data and coordinating responses if sensors indicated the possible presence of radioactive material.

A dirty bomb, also known as a radiological dispersal device, is designed to spread radioactive material using conventional explosives. Security officials have long warned that while such a device would be unlikely to cause destruction on the scale of a nuclear weapon, it could create panic, contaminate infrastructure and disrupt transportation and commerce.

During the exercise, patrol boats moved through designated areas of the harbor while operators monitored radiation-detection instruments. Other teams simulated follow-up procedures, including establishing safety zones, notifying command centers and dispatching specialized units trained to assess hazardous materials.

Officials emphasized that maritime security in New York relies heavily on coordination among agencies. The harbor includes ferry routes, cruise terminals, fuel depots, bridges, tunnels and cargo facilities, making communication between law enforcement, emergency responders and port operators essential.

Residents and commuters may have noticed an increased presence of law-enforcement boats and aircraft during the exercise, but officials said there was no danger to the public.

“These drills are about readiness,” an NYPD spokesperson said. “The goal is to detect threats early, respond safely and keep New Yorkers moving.”

New York City has expanded its radiation-detection capabilities in the years since the Sept. 11 attacks, deploying sensors at bridges, tunnels, major events and maritime checkpoints. Officials said the latest harbor exercise was intended to test both technology and interagency coordination in a realistic environment.

Additional training exercises are expected in the coming months as agencies continue to refine plans for responding to chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear threats in the region.

**Authorities Detect Radioactive Material During Six-Hour Harbor Security Drill**

*By CNN Staff*

**Port Harbor, Maryland** — Federal, state and local authorities completed a six-hour harbor security exercise Tuesday in which response teams simulated the discovery of radioactive material aboard a pleasure craft as part of a mock terrorist threat scenario, officials said.

The drill, conducted in and around Port Harbor Marina, involved the U.S. Coast Guard, local police and fire departments, emergency management officials, harbor patrol units and radiation safety specialists. Organizers said the exercise was designed to test coordination among agencies during a potential maritime security incident involving hazardous materials.

According to officials, the scenario began with a simulated intelligence bulletin warning of a possible threat to a waterfront event. Patrol crews then identified a privately owned recreational vessel that matched the fictional description provided in the exercise. After the boat was escorted to a secured area of the marina, trained hazardous materials personnel used radiation detection equipment and identified a sealed source containing Caesium-137, a radioactive isotope commonly used in industrial gauges and medical equipment.

Authorities emphasized that the material was part of a controlled training scenario and that there was no danger to the public.

“This was an exercise only,” Port Harbor Police Chief Daniel Reyes said at a briefing after the drill. “There was no real terrorist threat, no release of radioactive material and no risk to residents or visitors. The purpose was to make sure every agency knows its role if we ever face a real emergency.”

During the drill, law enforcement officers established a security perimeter, temporarily restricted boat traffic in part of the harbor and practiced evacuating a small section of the marina. Fire department hazardous materials teams assessed the vessel, while emergency medical personnel rehearsed screening and decontamination procedures for role players posing as passengers and dockworkers.

The Coast Guard said the exercise also tested communications between patrol boats, command centers and local emergency operations officials.

“Maritime threats require a unified response,” Coast Guard Lt. Cmdr. Alicia Morgan said. “A harbor is a complex environment, with commercial traffic, recreational boaters and nearby public spaces. Exercises like this help us identify gaps before an actual incident occurs.”

Caesium-137 can pose serious health risks if improperly handled or dispersed, but experts said sealed sources can be transported and secured safely by trained personnel. In Tuesday’s scenario, technicians practiced isolating the item, confirming readings and transferring custody to appropriate authorities.

Some nearby residents and boat owners said they were notified in advance that a drill would take place, though several visitors were surprised by the presence of emergency vehicles and patrol boats.

“I saw the Coast Guard and police boats moving in and thought something had happened,” said marina tenant Carla Simmons. “Once they explained it was a drill, it was reassuring to see how seriously they were taking it.”

Officials said normal harbor operations resumed shortly after the exercise concluded. A multiagency review is expected in the coming weeks to evaluate response times, communications and public notification procedures.

“This is exactly why we train,” Reyes said. “The goal is prevention, preparedness and public safety.”
